summary: Believable low scrubby mound with arching canes, but the leaves are maple/ivy-shaped, there is no fruit, and the canopy is too see-through to read as a bramble thicket.
critique: Silhouette is about right: a low dome roughly 1.5-2 m across with a few canes arching out and touching down at the tips, which is the correct bramble habit. Problems: (1) Leaf shape is wrong. The cards read as palmate, maple- or ivy-like single leaves. Bramble (Rubus fruticosus) has compound leaves with 3-5 serrated oval leaflets, matt dark green on top and paler and felty underneath. At the distances a game uses, the wrong outline is the main reason it reads as 'generic shrub'. (2) No blackberries. The tiny white flowers and a few isolated red leaves are not enough. A bramble is identified by clusters of green, red and black drupelet fruit or by dense white or pink 5-petal flowers. (3) Density: real brambles are an impenetrable tangle with no gaps. Here the brown mulch disc and the interior show clearly through the canopy from above, and the 3/4 views are sparse at the top edge. (4) Canes are too thin and too uniform pink-tan. Real first-year canes are 8-15 mm thick, angular, red-purple on the sun side and green underneath, with visible prickles. (5) The bare brown soil disc under the plant looks like a planting pit, not a hedge-bottom. (6) The scattered red leaves look like random tints, not autumn colour following a pattern (older, lower and outer leaves turning first). (7) Leaf cards are uniformly lit with no translucency or underside colour, so the mass looks flat.
suggestions: Redraw the leaf atlas as compound leaves: 3- and 5-leaflet rosettes, each leaflet an ovate blade with saw-tooth edges about 40-70 mm long. One 512x512 atlas with 4 variants, alpha-tested. Keep the card count; only the texture changes.

Add fruit clusters as small alpha cards or 6-8-triangle blobs in groups of 3-8 berries, mixed green, red and glossy black (albedo ~0.03, roughness ~0.25). Put them at cane tips and leaf axils. Cost is roughly 300-500 tris total.

Increase interior fill. Add 2-3 large inner 'mass' cards or a low-poly inner hull, shaded dark green (albedo ~0.05), so you never see soil through the top. Push 30% more leaf cards into the upper third.
Thicken the main canes to 8-12 mm, 5-sided tubes. Use a red-purple to green gradient along each cane. Add prickles as a tiny alpha strip or as normal-map dots on the cane UV.
Replace the bare soil disc with leaf litter and dead grass blended into the ground, or drop it and let the base canes root into the lawn.
Give leaves a paler, greyer underside (back-face albedo ~+15% and desaturated) and a little subsurface/translucency term. Drive red/brown autumn tint by height and age, not at random.
renderer_notes: The lawn is a flat tiled texture and the very soft sky ambient flattens foliage. Neither is the asset's fault.

summary: Correct 20 ft ISO proportions with good door gear and corner castings, but the corrugation is shallow and the wear is a pattern of black dash glitches that reads as a texture fault rather than damage.
critique: Proportions look right for a 20 ft dry box (6058 x 2438 x 2591). Door end is the strongest part: four locking bars with cam keepers, handles, hinge blocks, a CSC plate and a data panel. Corner castings have oval apertures, and rust patches on the roof are well placed near the corners. Weaknesses: (1) Side wall wear is a field of short horizontal and vertical black dashes, densest in the lower half. They look like z-fighting or a broken mask, not real paint damage. Real containers show scrapes that expose grey primer or orange rust, dents with streaky run-off below them, and faded, chalky paint. They do not show pure-black slots. (2) The corrugation depth is too shallow. Real side walls are trapezoidal, about 36 mm deep on roughly a 278 mm pitch, so the top and bottom side rails and the silhouette at the corner posts should show a zig-zag profile with strong light-and-shadow banding. Here the sides read almost flat, especially in the side-on view. (3) The 'KESTREL' lettering has no paint texture. It is a uniform grey-white, while the rest of the container is weathered. (4) Door-end cam keepers are oversized cubes, and the locking bars look like round grey rods with no galvanised sheen. (5) No forklift pockets in the bottom side rails, which 20 ft boxes commonly have. No bottom rail or crossmember detail is visible, and no dents. (6) Blue paint is evenly saturated everywhere, with no sun-fading on the roof and upper sides.
suggestions: Remove the black-dash wear mask. Replace it with three wear layers: (a) edge and rail chips showing brown rust (albedo ~0.25,0.12,0.06) with a primer-grey rim; (b) vertical rust and dirt streaks under each chip and under the roof rail, 0.5-1.2 m long, fading downward; (c) a broad sun-fade gradient, about 15% lighter and desaturated toward the roof. All three fit in one 1024 tiling detail plus the existing atlas.

Model the side corrugation as real geometry: a trapezoid profile 36 mm deep on a ~278 mm pitch (about 22 bays per 20 ft side). That is roughly 4 verts per bay per edge, so about 200 extra tris per side, which is cheap. Alternatively, keep it flat but bake a strong normal map and add the zig-zag cut-out at the corner-post silhouette.
Add the two forklift pockets in each bottom side rail of the 20 ft (about 350 x 115 mm openings, centres ~2050 mm apart). Add a visible bottom side rail lip about 160 mm tall.
Weather the KESTREL and ID decals with the same chip and fade mask, so the letters lose paint where the blue does.
Shrink the cam keepers to about 70 x 70 x 50 mm and give the locking bars a galvanised metal look (metallic 1, roughness ~0.45, albedo ~0.55) with some rust at the guides.
Add 2-4 random soft dents per side panel as normal-map blobs. Per-instance variation is cheap through a dent-atlas offset.
renderer_notes: Shadow and ambient are fine. The black dashes are in the texture or geometry, not the renderer.

summary: A convincing wild tussock with fine arching blades and flowering panicles. Close to good; needs blade width variety, dead thatch and more density at the base.
critique: Good read: fine, arching blades radiating from a tight crown, with a mix of green and straw-coloured blades and two or three flowering culms carrying open panicles (one purplish, one cream). It looks like a Deschampsia or Festuca tussock. Issues: (1) Blades are all the same very thin width, so at mid-distance the tuft looks wiry and thin, more like an ornamental grass than a field tussock. (2) The crown is sparse. Real tussocks have a dense, darker base packed with dead brown thatch and old leaf sheaths. Here the base is open and the same green as the rest. (3) The dry blades are pale grey-beige straight lines with no curl or twist. Dead grass blades curl, kink and lie flatter. (4) Panicle spikelets are small dots with no droop. Real flowering heads nod a little under their weight. (5) The flowering stems are long and stick up well above the tuft; about 2x the leaf height is fine, but they are too straight and stiff.
suggestions: Vary blade width from 2 to 6 mm and taper each blade to its tip. Use 3 width classes. Keep the blade count the same and widen about 40% of the cards.
Add a dense base: 8-12 short (50-120 mm) dark brown, crumpled thatch cards around the crown, plus a dark ambient-occlusion tint (albedo x0.5) on the lowest 30% of every blade.
Give dead blades a kink or curl (bend 2-3 segments past 60 degrees) so they lie outward on the ground instead of standing straight.
Bend the flowering culms so they nod 10-25 degrees at the top, and use 2-3 culms of different heights instead of matched pairs.
Add a light translucency/backlight term for blades seen against the sun. This costs nothing in geometry.
renderer_notes: The surrounding lawn is a coarse, blurry noise texture that makes any fine-grass asset look out of place. That is the lawn, not the tuft.

summary: A solid, believable mesh ball cage on castors with an open lid and a push handle. The frame is good. Ball inter-penetration, uniform mesh and clean paint keep it CG.
critique: Strong overall: green powder-coated tube frame, welded square mesh, hinged lid propped open, a push handle with a rubber grip, castors with red brake pedals, and about 14 mixed-colour balls inside. Proportions are about 1.1 m tall on a ~0.8 x 0.6 m footprint, which matches the reference. Issues: (1) Balls clip into each other (the yellow and orange balls on the lower layer visibly overlap) and some appear to rest in mid-air against the mesh. That breaks the physical read at close range. (2) Every ball uses the same truncated-icosahedron pattern with only a colour swap and no seams or brand text, so they look like clip art. (3) The mesh wire is perfectly regular and the same weight everywhere. There are no weld nodes, and nothing shows wire thickness versus tube thickness in shadow. (4) The paint is spotless, with no scuffs at the corners, castor mounts or handle. Training kit carts are always chipped and grass-stained at the bottom. (5) The lid has no stay or chain to hold it open; it just stands vertical. Its catch is a tiny white tab. (6) The castors are small and the forks are simple. That is fine, but they could use a tread.
suggestions: Pack the balls physically: place them by sphere-packing at 220 mm diameter, with no overlaps, each resting on the floor mesh or on 3 balls below. This is a generator change only, at no runtime cost.
Give the balls a 4-6 design atlas (different panel layouts and brand stripes, 512 px each, shared), plus dirt and grass-stain overlays. Add a subtle seam normal map. Rotate each ball randomly.
Add worn paint to the frame: chips showing grey galvanised steel at the top rails, handle ends and lid edges, and grass and mud staining on the bottom 150 mm. One tiling wear mask does this.
Add a lid stay: a short chain or flat bar from the lid corner to the frame, about 200 tris. Or angle the lid back to rest past vertical against a stop.
Add a small weld bead (a tiny sphere or normal dot) where the mesh meets the tube frame, and make the mesh wire about 4 mm against a 25 mm tube so the difference in thickness reads.
renderer_notes: The cast shadow of the mesh is clean. The grass carpet texture is coarse and noisy at close range, which is the renderer and ground, not the asset.

summary: Recognisable tip-up stadium seat on a pedestal with a pivot axle and a seat number, but the plastic shell is too thin and smooth and the mechanism is chunky and simplified.
critique: Correct concept: red polypropylene seat and back on a steel pedestal with a base plate and four anchor bolts, a cross axle with end caps, hinge brackets, and a seat-number plaque (27) on the back. The size reads as about right (a seat about 450-500 mm wide). Issues: (1) The shell is a uniform thin sheet. Real moulded seats are 4-6 mm wall with a thickened rolled rim, and the underside and back have deep moulded ribs (10-20 mm tall) in a grid, plus mould ejector marks. Here the 'ribs' are just engraved grooves, so the underside looks flat in the close-up. (2) Material is bright saturated red with a soft plastic sheen but no texture: no fine moulding stipple, no UV fade, no scuffs or dirty seat-pan centre. Stadium seats are visibly faded and grubby at the front lip and the seat centre. (3) The pivot mechanism is oversized and toy-like. The black hinge blocks look like plain cubes and the axle end caps like rubber wheels. Real tip-up seats use a slim metal bracket each side with a spring-return cover and small fixings. (4) From the side, the seat pan and back are both near vertical and the gap between them is odd. A folded seat pan should sit roughly parallel to and about 50-80 mm in front of the back. (5) Pedestal: a single central post is plausible for a riser-mounted seat, but the post is a plain box section with no welded gusset or chamfered top cap. (6) The seat number plaque is good, but there is no row or block label and no fixing rivets.
suggestions: Give the shell real thickness (4-6 mm) and a rolled rim (8-10 mm round edge) with a separate edge loop, and model a 3x3 rib grid on the underside as raised geometry 12 mm deep. That is about 300 extra tris per seat, acceptable for instanced seating, or put it in a normal map for the far LOD.

Material: albedo red around (0.45, 0.04, 0.04) linear, roughness 0.55 with a fine stipple normal. Add a per-instance fade (5-20% lighter and toward pink on the top surfaces) and a grime mask on the front lip and seat centre.
Slim the hinge hardware: brackets about 40 x 80 x 6 mm steel plate with two bolt heads, and a narrow sprung cover over the axle (Ø 30 mm), with no wheel-like end caps.
Fix the folded pose: the seat pan rotates to about 80 degrees from horizontal and parks 50-80 mm in front of the backrest with a consistent gap.
Add a pedestal top cap and a small gusset at the base plate. Put a powder-coat edge chip and a rust bloom at the bolts.
renderer_notes: The saturated red may be pushed a little by the tonemapper, but the lack of texture is the asset's.

summary: Clean, correctly proportioned 1.5 x 1 m training goal with elbow joints, net clips and ground pegs, but the net is a stiff wireframe of cord lines with no sag or knots, and the frame is factory-clean.
critique: The frame is good: about 1.5 x 1.0 m, white powder-coated round tube, moulded corner elbows, a sloped back frame running to a ground bar, net hooks along the crossbar, and black ground pegs. The silhouette reads correctly from all angles. Issues: (1) The net is the main giveaway. It is a perfectly rigid grid of thin grey lines, tight in every direction, with no catenary sag between attachment points, no knots at the intersections, and no slack bunching at the bottom bar. Real training nets are 3-4 mm braided polyethylene on about 100-120 mm squares, they hang loose, and they bulge at the back. (2) The net only fills the back and side planes, and the mesh spacing is too regular. (3) The frame has no wear. Mini goals on a training ground get grass and mud on the bottom bar, scuffs on the posts at ball height, and chipped paint at the elbows. (4) The tube looks a little thin for a 'steel' goal (it reads about 40 mm). The reference mentions 60 mm heavyweight steel versions, but 40-50 mm is fine for a portable goal. (5) The joints have plain sleeve bands with no visible bolts or pins.
suggestions: Rebuild the net as a sagged mesh: simulate or approximate catenary sag of 30-60 mm between clips, a bulge of about 80 mm on the back panel, and 100-150 mm of slack bunching at the ground bar. Keep it as anti-aliased cord ribbons, about 3.5 mm wide, with tiny knot nubs at the intersections (or a dot in the cord texture).
Add frame wear: green grass stain and brown mud on the bottom 100 mm of every ground-contact tube, scuffs on the uprights at 0.3-0.7 m, and grey metal chips at the elbows.
Show a bolt or spring pin at each elbow socket (a small cylinder and hex head, about 40 tris each).
Make the net colour slightly off-white or dirty grey with a roughness of about 0.8, and vary the line brightness so it stops reading as vector lines.
renderer_notes: The net already draws anti-aliased, which is good. The rest is the asset.

summary: Right 40 ft proportions and a shared door end, but it carries the same flat-looking corrugation and black-dash wear glitches as the 20 ft, and the long sides make the repetition and flatness more obvious.
critique: Proportions match ISO 40 ft (12192 x 2438 x 2591). The door end, corner castings and roof rust patches are shared with the 20 ft, which is good. On the long side the problems are amplified: (1) The black dash marks repeat across the whole 12 m wall and read clearly as a texture artefact. (2) The side corrugation is almost invisible in the side-on view, so the long wall looks like a flat blue slab. On a real 40 ft box this is a bold rhythm of about 44 bays. (3) The rust spots on the roof are random blots. Real roof wear pools in dents, along the cross-bows, and at the corners, with dark tea-stain run-off down the side rails. (4) The ID marking at the upper right is fine, but there is no CSC plate or capacity data on the side, and no gooseneck tunnel at the bottom of the front end. (5) The paint is perfectly uniform and saturated across 12 m, with no panel-to-panel variation from patch repairs. Real containers often have repainted panels in a slightly different blue.
suggestions: Same as for the 20 ft: replace the black-dash wear with rust chips, run-off streaks and sun fade.
Use real trapezoidal corrugation geometry (36 mm deep, ~278 mm pitch), about 450 tris per long side. On a 40 ft box this is the single biggest realism gain at range.
Add per-panel variation: 1-3 random repaired panels per side in a slightly different blue (hue shift ±5%, brightness ±10%), with a straight weld-line edge.
Add the gooseneck tunnel recess under the front (non-door) end: about 3.2 m long, 1 m wide and 120 mm deep, a cheap negative box.
Put the roof rust along the cross-bow lines and in 2-3 shallow dent hollows, and add rust-streak decals running down from the top side rail.
renderer_notes: No renderer problems beyond flat ambient.

summary: Reads as a weeping tree at a glance, but the crown is small and sparse on a thin, short trunk, and the hanging curtain stops well above the ground. Not yet a convincing mature weeping willow.
critique: Positive: a forked trunk, an open umbrella crown, pendulous strand curtains, and a two-tone yellow-green leaf colour that is right for Salix babylonica. Problems: (1) Form and scale. A mature weeping willow is 12-20 m tall with a 15-20 m spread and a massive, often leaning trunk 0.5-0.9 m in diameter, and the curtain sweeps all the way to the ground (often trailing on it). Here the curtain ends roughly one third of the tree height above the lawn, the trunk is slender and short, and the tree reads more like a young ornamental. (2) Density. The crown is very see-through. The shadow on the ground is almost pure branch skeleton with only faint speckle from the foliage. A real willow casts a dense, dappled pool of shade. The top-down view shows bare branches poking through the crown. (3) The strands read as dotted dither, not leafy whips. Each strand should be a continuous pendulous twig densely set with narrow lanceolate leaves 80-150 mm long. (4) There is an abrupt colour split: one half of the crown is dark olive and the other pale lime. That looks like inconsistent normals or two leaf materials, not lighting. (5) The main branches are thin, crooked sticks with too few orders of branching. Willow scaffolds are thick, rise upward and outward in a broad vase, then arch over. (6) The bark is a smooth brown. Willow bark is deeply furrowed and grey-brown.
suggestions: Rescale to a mature tree, about 14 m tall, with a crown spread of about 16 m, a trunk diameter of 0.7 m at 1.3 m height, and the first fork at 2-3 m. Lengthen the hanging strands so most end 0-0.5 m above the ground and some touch it.

Double to triple the strand density. Build strands as long vertical alpha cards (0.15-0.25 m wide and 2-6 m long) with a dense lanceolate-leaf texture, so the curtain is about 70% opaque. That is about 1,500-3,000 cards, about 6k tris, and fine for a hero tree with a billboard LOD.

Unify the leaf colour: one material, yellow-green albedo about (0.30,0.38,0.12), with a per-strand hue jitter of ±5%. Fix any flipped normals that cause the dark half (point foliage normals out from the crown centre).
Thicken the scaffold: 4-6 primary limbs 0.25-0.35 m diameter, rising at 40-60 degrees, then arching over. Add a second and third order of branching before the strands start.
Bark: grey-brown albedo about 0.18 with a deep vertical furrow normal map (1024 tiling) and a slight flare and lean at the trunk base.
Make the shadow casting use the same alpha as the strands, or add a coarse shadow-only proxy hull, so the ground gets a dense dappled shade pool.
renderer_notes: No GI or ambient occlusion makes the interior of any tree look too light. Even so, the sparseness is in the asset.
